Early nutrition can influence health for many years because the body and immune system develop quickly during the first stages of life.

Researchers compared people who experienced different food environments in childhood and followed their health outcomes over several decades.

The study found meaningful differences in later disease risk, biological ageing, and dietary habits among the groups.

These results do not prove that one food policy should be copied today, but they show why early exposure deserves careful study.

Why the finding matters

Long-term studies can reveal patterns that are difficult to see in short experiments, especially when later outcomes depend on habits formed much earlier.

The evidence supports more research into how nutrition, development, and social conditions interact throughout a person’s life.
